Government Says Stellantis Breaching Commitments

Stellantis is offering to repay some of the money that Canada's government wants to see returned for past support, but it won't say if it's prepared to defend in court the proposed sale of an Ontario plant.
The company said it will voluntarily return the C$24 million in federal government support it received for a planned retooling of its idled Brampton assembly plant in the Toronto area.

Following a meeting Thursday between the company, the union Unifor and government officials, Industry Minister Melanie Joly said Ottawa has issued a notice of default on a 2022 federal funding agreement. Joly said Stellantis was on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars. The minister has given the company 30 days to take "corrective action."
Cleveland-Cliffs to Recall Laid-Off Workers at Canadian Steel Operation
Cleveland-Cliffs will recall laid-off workers at its Stelco operation in Canada in response to improved customer demand.

The steelmaker said it will restart finishing operations at its Hamilton plant on Lake Ontario and bring back all 175 workers who were temporarily let go after the company reached support agreements with a sufficient volume of its customers.

Cliffs had been in a bitter war of words with Canada's government over the layoffs and was facing the threat of being dragged into court over accusations it wasn't living up to commitments made to secure approval for its roughly $2.4 billion acquisition of Stelco in 2024.
Wholesale Sales Rose 0.7% in September
Canadian wholesale trade recovered in September, driven by a rise in sales of computer and communications equipment and vehicle activity.

Wholesale sales rose 0.7% from the month before to a seasonally adjusted C$92.46 billion, Statistics Canada said. That was stronger than the data agency's advance estimate of a 0.5% rise following a drop of 1.4% the month before.
Still, the volume of sales in September was down 0.2%.
Compared with a year earlier, nominal wholesale sales increased 7.8%, while transactions on a volume basis were up a more subdued 1.5%, the data agency said.
Factory Sales Were Flat in September
Canadian manufacturing activity stalled in September despite a tailwind from higher energy prices, as a sharp drop in the volume of primary metals sold weighed heavily.

Factory shipments were little changed from the month before at a seasonally adjusted C$80.25 billion, Statistics Canada said. That was softer than the data agency's early estimate for a 0.1% rise after sales in August climbed by an upwardly revised 1.8%.
Compared with a year earlier, sales in September were up 10.9%.
Bombardier Gets Firm Order From Saudi Helicopter Company for Up to 60 Aircraft
Saudi Arabia's top commercial helicopter operator will buy a dozen aircraft from Bombardier worth about $568 million, part of a larger fleet purchase deal for up to 60 of the Canadian company's jets.
The â€‹Helicopter Company, owned by Saudi Public Investment Fund, signed a firm order for five of Bombardier's Challenger 3500 jets, five Global 5500s and two Global 8000 aircraft, Bombardier said.

The order includes options for an additional 48 jets, and marks the biggest business aviation fleet order to date in Saudi Arabia, part of the country's aim to develop the industry. The aircraft will form the foundation of THC's business aircraft fleet.
Triple Flag Precious Metals Renews Share-Buyback Program
Triple Flag Precious Metals plans to buy back the equivalent of 5% of its issued and outstanding shares over a one-year period has been accepted by the Toronto Stock Exchange.
The Canadian precious metals streaming and royalty company said the renewed normal course issuer bid authorizes it to repurchase up to 10.3 million of its shares through Nov. 16, 2027.
The shares may be bought on either the Toronto or New York stock exchanges, or alternative trading systems.
Onex Quarterly Earnings Up Sharply
Onex's earnings more than doubled in the latest quarter, bolstered by an increased gain on corporate investments.
The Canadian private-equity firm recorded third-quarter net earnings of $97 million, or $1.28 a share, up from $39 million, or 57 cents a share, a year earlier.

Distributable earnings--a measure of recurring fee-related earnings, realized gains from investments and the receipt of carried interest from private equity and private credit funds--fell to $89 million from last year's $111 million.
Stantec Shares Up on Raised Full-Year Adj EPS Outlook
Shares of Stantec rose after the company raised its adjusted earnings outlook and posted higher profit and revenue in the third quarter.
Shares climbed 13.8% to settle at C$122.20.
The engineering consulting company late Thursday posted a profit of $179.6 million, or $1.60 a share, compared with $150 million, or $1.32, the year earlier.
Adjusted earnings per share were $1.89, above the $1.77 expected by analysts polled by FactSet.
Honda to Receive $220 Million in Canadian Government Support for Plant Retooling

The Canadian government will help fund Honda's planned retooling of a plant in southern Ontario to expand the production of hybrid-electric vehicles in an effort to help secure jobs and support an auto industry that is still under pressure from U.S. tariffs.
The federal government said it will invest C$313 million, in the Alliston facility through its Strategic Response Fund.
Ontario's government will provide a further C$156 million to Honda's C$867 million development plans.
TALKING POINT
Railroad CEO's Loose Lips Threaten to Torpedo His $72 Billion Megadeal
By Esther Fung
Union Pacific's UNP chief executive may have tanked his own deal, a $71.5 billion plan to create a transcontinental railroad that he touted as the future of freight.

It goes back to private remarks Jim Vena made at an industry event in March. The ultracompetitive, tough-talking executive threatened anyone who spoke out against Union Pacific's proposed combination with Norfolk Southern NSC, which is currently awaiting regulatory approval.
"I'll probably increase everybody's rates that said they didn't want a seamless railroad by three or four extra percent to teach you a lesson," Vena said in a video recording of his remarks.

Union Pacific had spent months trying to prevent the recording from going public. Now that it is out, farmers, chemical makers and other opponents have amped up their warnings about the dangers of creating a rail giant with enormous pricing power.

Meanwhile, the Surface Transportation Board, the federal agency that must approve the deal, has moved to reassure all the companies, farms and unions that would be affected by the deal that it is taking into account the influence that threats can have on public comment. The board could make a decision whether to approve the deal in the middle of next year.

The board had ordered Union Pacific to release the video of Vena's remarks. Earlier this month, it said it has "serious concerns" that Vena's remarks may influence the willingness of those who would be affected by a merger to share their views for fear of commercial repercussions.

"Retaliation, whether perceived or actual, can seriously undermine the integrity of the Board's processes," it said. Any evidence or threat of retaliation, the board added, affects how it proceeds with the merger review.
Union Pacific said it doesn't retaliate against customers and that its chief executive had made an offhand comment. "Vena is known for being a dynamic speaker," the railroad said.

The stakes are high. A merger would create the country's first coast-to-coast railroad operated by a single company controlling 50,000 miles of tracks from the Jersey shore to California ports. Supporters say it would speed up shipping and make supply chains more efficient.
"This changes the dynamic for Union Pacific," said Robert Primus, a former chairman of the board. He said he also expects more scrutiny of the board.

Opponents, from the farmers, shippers and other firms that rely on rail service to the unions that represent rail workers, say a giant, powerful railroad would slack on service and drive up costs. The CEO's threat, they say, reinforces the downsides.

"Jim Vena crossed the line," said Chris Jahn, chief executive of the American Chemistry Council, which represents plastics and chemical companies. "Rail customers need competition and choice, not threats for speaking out against a bad deal."
At the helm of Union Pacific since 2023, Vena, 68, is known-and loved-on Wall Street for improving the company's performance and regularly surpassing rivals.

He is also known for sharp elbows and blunt talk. He laces earnings calls with talk about beating rivals on industry metrics like train length, speed and idle time. At a recent Morgan Stanley conference, he talked about running up hills with two female executives.

"I would have tripped one of them if I thought one of them was going to beat me," he said. "That's the way we should be here, OK?" he added. "Push the heck out of yourself and see what the heck you can do to win. I'm not here to be given second place."

During a keynote speech at the industry event where he made his controversial remarks, Vena first talked about besting his brother in racquetball in his 20s by realizing he could gain the advantage after hitting his brother with cross-court shots.
"He would give me a lot more space and would allow me to be able to make pass shots easier. So that's what I did. In fact, I hit him with the racket one day," Vena said.

The event, the Southwest Association of Rail Shippers conference in Houston, is an annual gathering every spring of hundreds of rail executives, consultants and academics who discuss services and the economic outlook. Railroads and their customers often meet on the side.

The proposed merger was a hot topic at the event. Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern say combining forces will cut shipping times and help customers better compete globally. Opponents say customers will be left with fewer alternatives when service is cut, shipments stall or rates spike.

"Come and see us, talk about what you need to move ahead with us and how we put this thing forward," Vena said during his speech. "If we don't do that, Union Pacific will still be there," he added, before saying he would probably be around, too, and threatened higher rates.

His remarks quickly ricocheted around the rail industry. Some shippers shared the comments with other railroad companies that oppose the merger. After catching wind, the Surface Transportation Board watched a video of Vena's speech over the summer.
Canadian Pacific Kansas City, a railroad that opposes the merger, petitioned the board to order Union Pacific to release the video. Union Pacific asked to keep the video confidential.

CPKC Chief Executive Keith Creel said the threats undermine the board's ability to review the merger, because it can't know whether customers gave honest feedback and won't be able to say it reached a sound decision based on hearing all concerns.

The regulators won't "ever know they're about to make a forever decision that all the forces against had been properly represented," Creel said during a recent earnings call. CPKC was the result of its own major rail merger, in 2023, between Canadian Pacific and Kansas City Southern.
Union Pacific said customers representing more than 30% of its volume support the merger. The company said it still believes in the merits of the deal and that it will get approved.

The Surface Transportation Board has extended the deadline for filing comments to Nov. 18. It invited commenters to pass along any threats or retaliation they faced and, in an uncommon move, told them that they have the option to provide their input confidentially.
